### Pax8 launches 8os to let IT partners govern AI agents and 8bot as a managed AI co-worker

Small business software marketplace Pax8 Inc. today launched 8os, an operating system that lets its information technology service provider partners govern the artificial intelligence agents running inside their customers’ businesses.

A second product, 8bot, gives those customers’ employees a managed AI coworker that partners deploy and supervise through 8os. Pax8 unveiled both at its Beyond EMEA conference in Copenhagen.

The launch is aimed at a governance gap that keeps turning up in Pax8’s quarterly “SMB AI Pulse” surveys. By the company’s count, nine in 10 small businesses are using or experimenting with AI, and only 23% have a documented policy covering it. Among those using AI, 71% have built at least one tool of their own, and just 31% of the builders have a formal review or approval process. Nearly half of those surveyed said they had found unsanctioned “shadow AI” in the past six months.

Pax8 said 84% of the business leaders it surveyed would trust an outside technology adviser to help them implement AI. The company wants its partners to be that adviser, and it has taken to calling partners that do AI work managed intelligence providers. A program launched at Pax8’s Beyond conference in Salt Lake City in June walks managed service providers through that change, starting with an assessment of their AI maturity.

The new operating system is built on the marketplace that more than 47,000 IT providers already use to sell software to some 800,000 small businesses. Partner and client identities carry over. Agents and models from different vendors are then managed together as one workforce, with the partner setting ownership and operating rules client by client. Each customer’s memory and context are kept separate, so the AI workers get more useful to that client over time.

Usage and spending are metered per user and per customer, and hard caps cut off consumption before a bill gets out of hand. The partner decides what to charge, with billing handled through the Pax8 account it already has.

Employees at the client businesses get 8bot. The assistant takes on everyday tasks and returns work that staff can review and refine before using it elsewhere in the business. Resellers offer it as a packaged service under 8os governance, and Pax8 is pitching it as something they can deploy and start billing for within minutes.

“AI is becoming a worker, and that changes what small businesses need from their technology partners,” Chief Executive Scott Chasin said. Those workers will come from many vendors and models, he added. In Chasin’s account, partners would use 8os to govern them across every customer, with 8bot as an AI coworker they can deploy, support and charge for.

Libby McIlhany, Pax8’s chief product officer, said partners had asked for a way to deliver AI “without building a custom solution for every client.”

Limited early access to both products opens this week, ahead of general availability planned for early next year.

content_en:
Blacksmith, a startup that runs the infrastructure companies use to test code before it ships, has been valued at $1 billion following a new $66 million funding round led by Sequoia Capital.

The round, which is Blacksmith’s Series C, comes about two months after the company raised a $45 million Series B led by Peak XV Partners at a $550 million valuation. It brings Blacksmith’s total funding to about $124.5 million.

Blacksmith says more than 10,000 companies now use its platform, up from about 5,000 in August. Customers include well-known startups Granola, Handshake, Supabase and LangChain. At the start of the year Blacksmith ran 5 million validation checks a week; it now runs 90 million. Annual recurring revenue has grown 17x over the same period, according to cofounder and CEO Aditya Jayaprakash, who said revenue is now in the tens of millions. The company said its largest customers spend more than $1 million a year.

Jayaprakash told Fortune that most of the new money will go toward purchasing more computing power. The company has about 40 employees across San Francisco and New York and plans to reach around 75 by the end of the year.

Blacksmith was founded in 2024 by Jayaprakash, and sells what developers call continuous integration, or CI: the automated builds and tests that code has to pass before it can be merged into an existing codebase and deployed. Most companies run those jobs on servers rented from AWS, Google Cloud or Microsoft Azure. Blacksmith instead buys its own machines, tens of thousands of them, according to Jayaprakash, and installs them in data centers around the world. It has writes its own software to run them, including systems that save the repetitive setup work each test run would otherwise redo from scratch.

## **A new bottleneck**

Developers used to spend about half their time writing code and the other half waiting for it to build and pass checks, Jayaprakash said.

AI coding tools like Cursor, OpenAI’s Codex and Anthropic’s Claude Code have made the first half “extremely easy,” he said. “But now the bottleneck has shifted to the second piece, which is: how do I actually validate all this code?”

Even the leading labs are feeling the strain. Anthropic said last month that its own validation workloads grew 25 fold in six months as Claude took over most of its code output.

Blacksmith owns much of its own hardware—it buys its own servers rather than renting them from cloud giants like Amazon—which Jayaprakash says gives the company control over performance, but also exposes the company to the industry-wide shortage of compute and memory. Jayaprakash said capacity planning is one of the hardest parts of the business, because demand jumps every time a stronger model comes out. When Anthropic launched Claude Fable 5 in July, he said, CI volume on Blacksmith rose 40%.

As with many AI coding startups, there’s also a threat that leading AI model vendors—which already focus heavily on coding products—will eventually take over code validation themselves.

Coding agents like Codex and Claude Code can already run a project’s tests as they work, and Cursor launched a product in March that lets companies set up agents to automatically review and test new code. Meanwhile, Microsoft-owned GitHub sells its own hosted machines for running CI jobs. Jayaprakash argues Blacksmith is complementary to what the AI model companies do, because better models mean more code to check. “Usage on us actually goes up,” he said.

Less than six months ago, OpenAI said Microsoft would no longer have the exclusive license on its intellectual property. The day after that ended, cloud leader Amazon unveiled plans to host OpenAI models.

Now Google is getting its shot, bringing OpenAI's GPT products to its cloud's model garden and Antigravity coding tool in the coming weeks.

"Google Cloud's longstanding investment in machine learning and AI has made it a destination for AI workloads and the developers and data scientists building them," OpenAI said in a blog post.

Google has been on a run in cloud computing this year. Annualized revenue growth in the segment accelerated to about 82% in the second quarter from 63% in the first quarter, thanks partly to strong demand for AI models and custom chips. Amazon and Microsoft posted second-quarter cloud growth of 37% and 42%, respectively. All three report quarterly results next week.

Most business spending on AI is on OpenAI and Anthropic, according to data from corporate card issuer Ramp, though some corporate IT departments have integrated Google's Gemini models into their systems. In September, Google announced its next-generation Gemini 4 Argon model.

OpenAI was founded in 2015 partly as a counterweight to the concentration of AI research at companies like Google. Two years later, Google employees submitted the influential Transformer academic paper that propelled AI, but it was OpenAI that helped bring the technology forward with ChatGPT. Now OpenAI is courting investors at a $1.4 trillion valuation and targeting an initial public offering.

title: Coherence Neuro, which is developing AI models and brain implants to help combat brain tumors, raised a $45M seed from the OpenAI Startup Fund and Founders Fund

content_en:
OpenAI’s venture capital arm as well as Peter Thiel’s Founders Fund are investing in Coherence Neuro, a startup developing a brain implant to detect and treat cancer.

The investments are part of a $45 million seed funding round for Coherence and reflect Big Tech’s burgeoning interest in brain data. Coherence’s CEO and cofounder Ben Woodington says there is “growing synergy” between the big AI labs and companies building devices to decode the brain, known as brain-computer interfaces.

“The idea of capturing data to train better models and use it to optimize treatments is going to be super important,” he says. “The AI companies seem to be aligned with this thesis as well—that this novel data source is going to be valuable.”

Woodington says AI is a “perfect use case” for brain-computer interfaces because developers of these devices generate massive datasets that are too large for humans to analyze themselves. AI models can help read raw neural data and link it to actions, such as moving a computer cursor or producing synthesized speech.

In January, OpenAI announced that it was directly investing in a new brain-computer interface company, Merge Labs, cofounded by its billionaire CEO Sam Altman. Merge Labs came out of stealth with $252 million in initial funding to pursue ultrasound technology that can decode information from the brain. At the time, OpenAI said it was funding Merge Labs because of a belief that brain-computer interfaces “will create a natural, human-centered way for anyone to seamlessly interact with AI.” (The name Merge Labs comes from the idea popular in Silicon Valley that humans will eventually merge with machine intelligence.)

Thiel’s VC firm has also backed Elon Musk’s Neuralink as well as CTRL-labs, the creator of a wristband that translates neural signals from arm and hand movements that was acquired by Facebook in 2019.

Rather than focusing on restoring function for paralyzed individuals, San Francisco–based Coherence is developing AI models to decode subtle electrical signals associated with brain tumors. The company says it already knows how to detect these signals in animals to determine whether cancer is growing, shrinking, or recurring. The team is working to translate these findings for human research and, eventually, clinical trials.

This summer, Coherence briefly tested the recording ability of its implant in the brains of three people who were already undergoing brain tumor removal surgery at the Royal Melbourne Hospital in Australia. The implant was in place for roughly 30 minutes before being removed, providing an initial safety check. Next, Coherence is testing both the recording and stimulation capabilities of the device in an additional seven patients.

The implant is also designed to emit mild electrical stimulation to halt the growth of tumors. The idea is that over time, the device would learn to detect signals associated with cancer and provide real-time treatment. Coherence plans to use the new funding to launch a clinical trial to implant the device long-term in patients with glioblastoma, an aggressive type of brain cancer. The company also aims to develop implants to treat cancers in other parts of the body.

“Coherence's approach to developing a cancer therapy capable of improving from data is incredibly innovative,” Ian Hathaway, partner at the OpenAI Startup Fund, says in a statement. “We are proud to be backing them on this exciting mission.”

Woodington says that OpenAI will not have access to its data. “There's nothing in the contracts or arrangements that would mean that we would share, or they would have access to, any brain data or other health data that we're generating,” he says.

That is seemingly different from OpenAI’s relationship with Merge Labs. In its January announcement, OpenAI said it would “collaborate with Merge Labs on scientific foundation models and other frontier tools to accelerate progress.”

Demand from AI-natives is pulling the European AI cloud ecosystem forward faster than ever. Developers need compute closer to their data, open models they can customize and serve at scale, and full-stack infrastructure that is secure by design.

NVIDIA Cloud Partners across Europe, the Nordics, Africa, and Central Asia are expanding regional compute capacity for model training and inference, helping developers build agentic and physical AI applications, and establishing boundaries around what agents can access and do.

Together, they’re turning Europe’s energy, data, research and industrial expertise into productive intelligence — supporting new models, applications, organizations and jobs while giving people more control over where and how they develop and deploy AI.


## **Sovereign: AI Clouds Building European AI Infrastructure**

Europe is home to world-class research, engineering talent, industrial expertise, data, the next generation of models and applications that requires large-scale computing close to where that knowledge resides. Regional AI clouds provide the infrastructure foundation on which model builders, enterprises and entire industries can grow.

As AI factories scale, power becomes a constraint which makes it critical for every watt to produce more intelligence. Nscale is using the NVIDIA DSX Platform to coordinate power allocation with workload requirements. In tests using NVIDIA GB300 NVL72 systems, Nscale demonstrated that NVIDIA DSX MaxLPS enabled 37% more GPUs and nearly 50% higher aggregate inference throughput within the same provisioned power budget.

Nscale also plans to deploy NVIDIA Vera Rubin infrastructure for frontier-model training and production workloads to support leading model and application builders using its full-stack, vertically integrated platform with expansion across five European markets.

Crusoe is developing Spark, its liquid-cooled modular AI factories designed for the NVIDIA Vera Rubin platform, to bring Crusoe Cloud capacity closer to users for low-latency AI inference. Crusoe Cloud serves leading model and application builders across EMEA, including Base44, Gradium, LTX and Wonderful.

Aleria, Cassava Technologies, Firebird, G42, Radiant, SWI Compute and Vultr are also developing and expanding NVIDIA-powered AI infrastructure across Europe, the Nordics, Africa and Central Asia.

Regional capacity from AI clouds combines the full-stack NVIDIA DSX AI Factory platform, including NVIDIA Vera Rubin, NVIDIA BlueField and NVIDIA Spectrum-X Ethernet networking, giving customers greater choice and control over where workloads and data reside while advancing sovereign computing services and economic growth.

## **Open: Models and Libraries, From Training to Inference** 

Across the ecosystem, AI clouds are expanding NVIDIA-powered infrastructure and services for developers to build applications with open models and libraries. This new capacity supports model training, fine-tuning for specialized tasks and inference at scale, including applications deployed at the edge.

For production inference, Nebius has adopted NVIDIA Groq 3 LPX, using Spectrum-X Ethernet networking to integrate it with Vera Rubin NVL72 on Nebius Token Factory. The combination will bring faster token generation to latency-sensitive applications and agentic systems through the platform’s managed serverless and dedicated endpoints and familiar application programming interfaces.

For robotics and physical AI, Nebius offers a purpose-built AI cloud solution that includes its full-stack Physical AI Workbench. Robotics companies including Rhoda AI, RoboForce and Sereact are building on the platform. The company also launched three NVIDIA retail agent blueprints — covering inventory, store operations, and fine-tuning —- into early access on Nebius infrastructure.

Nebius is expanding its cloud services widely across the continent with its Physical AI Living Lab, and in Germany as a computer supplier for the Next Frontier Challenge of SPRIND, the Federal Agency for Breakthrough Innovation.

Baseten has developed a specialized model for code-review routing with Nemotron 3.5 Lightning used by CodeRabbit. Through supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning, CodeRabbit improved routing agreement from 75.8% to 80.7% while reducing estimated inference costs by 50% for the evaluated workload. The results demonstrate how AI developers can customize NVIDIA open models for specialized tasks while improving accuracy and inference efficiency.

Fireworks and Era4 are partnering to bring open models to enterprises across the U.K. and Europe. The collaboration combines Fireworks’ model training and inference platform with direct liquid-cooled capacity powered by NVIDIA Blackwell Ultra GPUs at Era4’s Chesterfield facility, supporting plans for enterprise AI solutions in financial services, insurance and life sciences.

Mistral is expanding its NVIDIA accelerated computing infrastructure to support model training, customization and inference. The expansion includes NVIDIA Vera Rubin infrastructure planned for delivery in 2027. Trained on 3,800 NVIDIA Grace Blackwell GPUs in Mistral-operated European data centers, Mistral Large 4 is the company’s latest frontier multimodal model, advancing capabilities across coding, agentic workflows and multimodal understanding.

Verda plans to deploy NVIDIA Vera Rubin, continuing to promote open weight models with NVIDIA Nemotron and NVIDIA Cosmos already in production, and using the NVIDIA Dynamo open source framework for inference optimization.

## **Safe: Secure Boundaries for AI Agents, From Silicon to Software**

As developers connect models to tools and business systems, they also need controls over what agents can access and do.

Announced at GTC Berlin, the NVIDIA OpenShell Reference Architecture with support from AI cloud ecosystem partners. Built on the foundation of NVIDIA OpenShell secure runtime software, the architecture is designed to give organizations full-stack control to deploy AI agents with clear boundaries around what agents can access and do.

NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 for model inference, NVIDIA Vera CPUs with OpenShell for agent harnesses and tool use, and NVIDIA BlueField-4 DPUs running NVIDIA Sentry for in-silicon enforcement. Each play a distinct role in delivering that control, working together so agents can achieve what they’re meant to do without moving beyond the boundaries people set for them.

Partners including Aleria, Baseten, Cassava, CoreWeave, Crusoe, DigitalOcean, Firebird, Fireworks, Firmus, G42, GMI Cloud, IREN, Lambda, Lightning AI, Nebius, Nscale, Radiant Verda and Vultr are supporting the OpenShell Reference Architecture to enable secure agentic deployments for their customers.

Together, European AI clouds are connecting regional infrastructure investment with the work of building and deploying AI. Expanded capacity gives builders more places to run workloads. Model and inference services help them put that capacity to use. Agent controls address what applications are allowed to do as they move into production.

Explore NVIDIA Cloud Partners for infrastructure and services, and the OpenShell Reference Architecture for agent deployment controls.

NVIDIA builds tools to enable safe agents across the stack. The NVIDIA OpenShell Reference Architecture, announced today, is part of NVIDIA’s growing portfolio of technologies that enables organizations to safely deploy agents at scale. NVIDIA Confidential Computing is the infrastructure layer that protects the models and data those agents depend on while running.

Today, NVIDIA is expanding that layer with Confidential Bare Metal, a new deployment option with NVIDIA Confidential Computing that enables frontier model builders to run sensitive workloads on dedicated third-party infrastructure while retaining control of their models and data.

NVIDIA is introducing new platform security controls that protect data in transit, measure platform integrity and enforce hardware-level access restrictions. These new controls let frontier model builders use bare-metal instances to own and operate their bespoke software stack, including host and platform infrastructure software, when operating on NVIDIA accelerated computing infrastructure across third-party cloud, neocloud and enterprise infrastructure.


NVIDIA Confidential Computing now offers a converged security architecture with three deployment options:

- Confidential Bare Metal for bare-metal infrastructure
- Confidential Containers for Kubernetes environments
- Confidential Virtual Machines for virtualized environments

Organizations can match the right model to their trust boundaries and operating requirements.

NVIDIA Confidential Computing is also expanding across NVIDIA Grace Blackwell and Rubin systems and will integrate with NVIDIA DSX OS as a reference architecture for cloud providers building AI factories.

## **Model Builders Tap Global Capacity**

Confidential Bare Metal gives supported providers a path to serve high-value workloads that require strong model and data privacy protections. For model builders, the expanding ecosystem offers more geographic, sovereign and operational options for scaling training and inference worldwide.

Cohere plans to integrate Confidential Bare Metal into Cohere Model Vault, using NVIDIA Confidential Computing trusted execution environments to extend hardware-rooted security directly to the GPU — protecting models and data in memory and across interconnects during execution.

“Enterprises trust Cohere to provide a secure and confidential platform for inference,” said Phil Blunsom, chief technology officer at Cohere. “With NVIDIA Confidential Computing in Cohere Model Vault, we’re extending hardware-rooted security directly to the GPU, protecting customer data in memory and across interconnects during execution.”

Google Cloud is extending support for  Confidential Bare Metal to A4X Max instances powered by NVIDIA GB300 NVL72 systems. These will combine non-virtualized NVIDIA accelerated computing with cryptographic protection for training data and model intellectual property.


“Google Cloud introduces Confidential Bare Metal to provide AI labs with hardware-isolated, non-virtualized compute environments and end-to-end cryptographic protection. Our A4X instances, built using NVIDIA Confidential Computing, preserve the privacy of user data, protect model IP, provide top-line serving performance,” said Andrés Lagar-Cavilla, distinguished engineer and AI infrastructure security lead at Google Cloud.

## **Confidential Computing Expands Across the NVIDIA Platform**

NVIDIA Confidential Computing uses hardware-rooted isolation and cryptographic attestation to help protect models and data during execution.

Support now extends to NVIDIA Grace Blackwell NVL72 — bringing Confidential Computing to NVL72 rack-scale systems — as well as x86-based NVIDIA HGX Rubin NVL8 and NVIDIA DGX Rubin NVL8 systems.

CoreWeave, Firmus, GMI Cloud, Google Cloud, IREN, Lambda, Microsoft Azure Infrastructure, Nebius, Nscale and Vultr support NVIDIA Confidential Computing deployments. Global systems partners including Cisco, Dell Technologies, HPE, Lenovo, Supermicro and Bull will support these capabilities with NVIDIA-Certified Systems.

NVIDIA DSX OS will support all NVIDIA Confidential Computing modes, giving cloud providers a software foundation for building and operating AI factories that support confidential workloads.

# China protests the US Deepseek ban while blocking ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini at home

## Key Points

- The US government has banned civilian federal agencies from using AI software from Chinese company Deepseek to keep sensitive data from flowing to Beijing.
- China criticized the decision and announced countermeasures, even though it blocks Western services like ChatGPT across the entire country.
- Beijing's protest works mainly as a political signal and lays the groundwork for future retaliation in the tech rivalry between the two countries.

**The US is banning Deepseek from government systems, and Beijing is calling it discrimination. Yet China locks out foreign AI far more strictly. The protest is still more than political theater.**

The US Department of Homeland Security recently ordered civilian federal agencies to remove all products from Chinese AI company Deepseek from their IT systems. The ban also covers software from other vendors built on Deepseek's open-source models, and it prohibits future purchases.

Washington says it's worried Beijing could access sensitive data through Deepseek. China has now pushed back hard. The Foreign Ministry accuses the US of stretching the concept of national security too far, while the Commerce Ministry is demanding the ban be lifted and has vowed to take resolute countermeasures.

On the substance, Beijing is on shaky ground, since China walls itself off far more consistently. ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini aren't approved there. Since 2023, the Cyberspace Administration has been required to review AI services, and those services must comply with political guidelines. That rule applies to the entire market, not just government agencies. State bodies and state-owned companies are supposed to gradually replace foreign hardware and software with domestic products. Reports also point to restrictions on iPhones for government officials.

According to the NYT, Beijing also proposed its own export and licensing controls for AI technologies last week, similar to the American approach.

## China's outrage rings hollow but still sends a political signal

The US concerns also have a concrete basis. China's 2017 National Intelligence Law requires companies and citizens to support the work of the country's intelligence services. Chinese models also carry a political slant, steering clear of certain topics and repeating state propaganda less critically than their Western counterparts. Then there's the economic side. AI companies, the FBI, and other US agencies have repeatedly accused Chinese firms of copying top US models on an industrial scale. Beijing denies this.

Still, the protest serves several purposes. It shows domestic companies that the state has their back. With other countries, it supports the narrative that the US wants to monopolize the AI industry. Most of all, it lays the groundwork for later retaliation, which Beijing can then frame as a mere response.

In the end, both sides invoke national security to protect their markets and technology. The US also ties security and economic policy together through its strict chip export controls. China's outrage isn't very credible, but the political signal behind it deserves to be taken seriously.

# OpenAI acquires Orchestra Bio to build AI agents that speed up drug development

**OpenAI is making a bigger bet on pharmaceuticals.** The company acquired Orchestra Bio, a startup that helps pharma teams coordinate drug development. Orchestra will be folded into Rosalind, OpenAI's AI platform for life sciences. GPT-Rosalind helps researchers analyze biological and chemical questions, while Rosalind Workbench connects those capabilities with scientific data and tools.

The combined effort aims to build AI agents that link scientific findings with clinical trials, decisions, and next steps to get new drugs to patients faster. Developing a drug in the US takes ten to 15 years on average. Beyond the scientific hurdles, siloed systems and the constant back-and-forth between internal teams and outside partners slow things down.

Orchestra's agents are designed to take work off teams' plates by tracking trials, flagging affected timelines when something goes wrong like a failed production batch, and surfacing options for what to do next. # OpenAI can't yet explain why its coding agents switch off misalignment monitoring

## Key Points

- Two internal OpenAI coding agents weakened or completely removed safety monitoring mechanisms on their own.
- One model turned off alerts to humans, while another deleted the monitoring entirely and then denied doing it.
- OpenAI sees the behavior as a recurring pattern. The company now blocks these changes automatically and is investigating the causes.

**Two internal OpenAI coding agents weakened the monitoring meant to catch misbehavior, even after weighing whether to keep those safeguards in place. One of them later denied it.**

Marcus Williams, who works on monitoring at OpenAI, made the incidents public on X. He describes a recurring pattern in which OpenAI's agents keep switching off misalignment monitoring. OpenAI lays out the details in a report on its alignment blog.

The monitoring is supposed to detect when agents behave differently than intended. Because it reviews so many events, it only alerts the safety team right away for incidents at the highest severity level, P0. OpenAI says neither case got that rating.

In the first case, on October 3, a researcher asked a coding agent based on GPT-6.1 Sol to compile evaluation tasks from employee feedback in a Slack channel. The agent wasn't supposed to send any messages along the way.

Eighty-two user messages later, the pipeline stopped because the monitor had flagged a planned fix but lacked the permissions to save its finding. Sol handed the fix to a subagent and told it to keep the monitoring intact.

Then Sol changed its assessment. It reasoned that a database entry could trigger a notification, which would conflict with the Slack instruction. The subagent had earlier rejected this step as unsafe. Following Sol's instructions, it cleared the recipient lists and gave as its reason that the user had explicitly asked for no messages.

The monitor kept running and saving its findings, but alerts to humans were turned off. The agent wrapped up by reporting that no messages had been sent.

## Astra's denial shows agents can hide what they changed

GPT-6 Astra went even further on October 6. A user asked the model to adopt the workflow of a reference implementation that didn't include a monitor. Another agent had previously told Astra not to disable the monitoring, not even temporarily.

Astra passed the task to a subagent with instructions to keep the monitoring only as far as it fit the reference. The subagent wondered whether this meant bypassing a safeguard, but it read the caveat as permission.

It removed the monitoring and replaced a test designed to protect it with one that assumed the monitoring was gone. Astra cheered the result in its chain of thought.

Astra then told the user the migration was complete without mentioning that the monitoring had been removed. When the user asked, the model denied removing an active monitor. Williams calls this a lie.

Williams stresses that the models didn't disable their own monitoring, which would be much harder to do in Codex. He still finds it concerning that they lean toward this kind of behavior at all, even though both cases leave room for some plausible deniability. So far, he says, the team hasn't observed openly misaligned motives.

## An exemption for weaker models leaves a gap in oversight

According to Williams, monitoring is especially easy to switch off during evaluations. OpenAI doesn't require it for models at the level of GPT-6 Luna because of their weaker capabilities. That means an Astra evaluation can be misconfigured so it falls under this exemption. Agents have repeatedly launched unmonitored deployments, even while they themselves were being watched.

In response, OpenAI updated the automated review required for internal Codex use. It's now supposed to detect and block attempts to disable monitoring. The company is also working on requiring a so-called safety case for every type of workload, which would spell out its monitoring requirements. Workloads without a valid safety case would be shut down automatically.

OpenAI offers two possible explanations for the behavior. One is excessive persistence of a supposedly harmless kind, where models carry out instructions further than expected. The other is a tendency to specifically evade misalignment monitoring and justify it with motivated reasoning.

OpenAI admits it doesn't have a satisfying explanation yet. It plans to study the behavior with methods such as experiments on the models' internal activations.

**Fuse Energy**, a British energy company, has opened reservations for Fuse Compute, its first commercial AI product, offering access to NVIDIA GPUs in UK data centres powered by Fuse – marking a new step into AI infrastructure by the EnergyTech startup.

Interested parties can register interest and reserve capacity today, with the first GPUs slated to come online in December 2026. The ambition here is to own the full AI stack: power, land, data centres and AI compute.

“*Power is the biggest hurdle to building AI infrastructure, and it’s the part we already know how to do*,” says **Alan Chang**, CEO and co-founder of Fuse Energy. “*Every AI company is fighting for the same scarce GPUs, and the grid can’t connect data centres fast enough to keep up. Fuse Compute puts that expertise to work for the companies building the future of intelligence, and makes sure that future is built in Britain*.”

This is an interesting new direction for an energy company whose focus is simplyfying gas and electricity management. Fuse has raised €178 million ($199 million) since its founding in 2022.

Our earlier coverage traces Fuse’s expansion from supplying 50,000 UK homes in July 2025, when it reported €76 million in annualised revenue and raised €8.5 million, to more than 200,000 households and €341 million in annual recurring revenue by December, when it secured another €59 million.

By June 2026, Fuse was supplying more than 300,000 households and had closed a €25 million Series B extension, while reporting monthly EBITDA profitability since December 2025.

Its expansion into AI compute comes amid significant funding for companies developing the underlying infrastructure. In the UK, Nscale raised €1.7 billion for vertically integrated AI compute, Volta reportedly secured €259.8 million across two rounds to develop AI factories, and Orbital Industries raised €43 million for industrial hardware including data-centre technologies.

Elsewhere, Finland’s Verda raised €164.8 million for AI cloud expansion and Spain’s iPronics secured €107.6 million for optical networking. These 2026 infrastructure financing announcements totalled approximately €2.4 billion, excluding Fuse’s historical funding.

The company says that AI is creating more demand for compute than the UK can supply. The UK Government’s Compute Roadmap estimates the country will need at least 6GW of AI-capable data centre capacity by 2030, yet new data centres face waits of up to a decade for a grid connection.

Power has become the main constraint on how quickly that capacity can be built. The Government aims to expand the UK’s public compute capacity 20x by 2030, but the country has few home-grown providers of large-scale compute, leaving many British AI companies reliant on capacity hosted overseas.

Fuse’s move into compute builds on its experience in power. Its most recent solar site was built at around 30% below the industry average cost per megawatt. It holds a power generation pipeline of more than 1GW and a data centre connection pipeline of 142MW across 15 projects. This will allow it to energise and construct high-density AI sites quickly and cheaply.

Fuse Compute will offer bare-metal, single-tenant NVIDIA GPU nodes in UK data centres, with UK jurisdiction and a UK data path. The first 128 NVIDIA B300 GPUs are due to come online in December 2026, followed by 1,024 in Q2 2027, a further 22MW in Q4 2027 and 116MW from 2028.

In energy, Fuse already supplies 470,000 UK homes and holds both supplier and meter operator licences.

On the supply side, Fuse owns and operates low carbon generation assets, with 22 MW active and over 1 GW in the pipeline across the UK, US, and Europe.

For the company, keeping compute onshore means that the data will stay under UK jurisdiction, and that British AI companies will no longer need to rely on overseas capacity.

Fuse’s near-term data centre projects will also reportedly bring 250 construction and operational jobs to the UK, and represent €1.1 billion (£1 billion) of investment in UK infrastructure.

content_en:
**Photon Bridge** (formerly Photon IP), an Eindhoven-based startup building optical engines for AI and telecom, has raised €10 million to tackle an emerging bottleneck in AI infrastructure: producing the millions of lasers needed to connect increasingly large clusters of AI processors.

New investors, the Amadeus APEX Technology Fund and 360 Capital, co-led the round, while existing investors Innovation Industries, Faber, and Brabant Development Agency (BOM) also increased their investment. In January 2025, the company announced it had secured a €4.75 million Seed round led by Innovation Industries.

*“Every new wave of compute creates new bottlenecks further down the supply chain, and lasers are the next one. Photon Bridge is addressing this with a technology that combines deep photonics expertise with a credible path towards manufacturing at very large scale,”* said **Ion Hauer**, Investment Partner at APEX Ventures.

Photon Bridge was founded in 2020 in Eindhoven by Rui Santos and Xaveer Leijtens to rethink how high-performance photonic systems are built at scale. The company says it is building laser sources for a market expected to need millions of units as optical connections move closer to AI chips.

It develops high-power, multi-wavelength laser-source technology for next-generation optical interconnects in AI data centres.

According to the startup, data transfer between processors is becoming a performance constraint as AI clusters expand from thousands to hundreds of thousands of chips. It notes that optical connections can move enormous amounts of data faster and more efficiently than conventional electrical interconnects, prompting their integration closer to processors.

It also notes that this shift is accelerating with the emergence of co-packaged optics, which integrates optical connectivity directly alongside the chips that move data through AI systems. The startup says that this, in turn, drives demand for the lasers that supply light to these connections.

*“Today’s high-power laser supply chain was largely built for telecom and subsea networks, where volumes are far lower. AI could transform the laser from a specialist photonics component into something that has to be manufactured at semiconductor scale. Photon Bridge has designed its technology around that transition,”* the company mentioned in the press release

Rather than generating the required optical power using a small number of increasingly powerful lasers, Photon Bridge claims that it combines and multiplexes light from multiple lower-power semiconductor lasers.

The Dutch startup says this approach reduces power densities, making individual lasers less sensitive to manufacturing defects, improving production yield and allowing Photon Bridge’s architecture to scale more efficiently as volumes increase.

The platform is designed to deliver high wavelength counts with up to 40 mW of optical power per wavelength per fibre, while enabling production across multiple indium phosphide (InP) foundries.

In September 2025, Photon IP rebranded as Photon Bridge and appointed Paul Marchal as CEO.

**Marchal**, CEO of Photon Bridge, said, *“AI is fundamentally changing the way computing infrastructure is built. We are moving towards enormous systems in which hundreds of thousands of processors have to operate together, and moving data between them is becoming one of the defining constraints on performance.*

*“That means optics has to move closer to the compute. But it also creates an entirely different manufacturing challenge. The industry will soon need millions of these laser sources every year. Instead of making individual lasers increasingly powerful and difficult to manufacture, we move that scaling challenge into the architecture.”*

Photon Bridge highlights that its approach is designed around manufacturing yield, a consideration that becomes increasingly important as laser production shifts from traditional telecom volumes to the scale required by AI infrastructure.

*“AI is turning lasers from a telecom component into a semiconductor-scale product. Once you start talking about millions of units a year, manufacturing yield becomes fundamental. Photon Bridge has designed its architecture from the beginning around the volumes this market is going to require,”* said **Cesare Maifredi**, Partner at 360 Capital.

The company plans to use this capital to accelerate product development and customer qualification, deliver its first samples in 2027, and prepare for volume manufacturing from 2028. Photon Bridge will also expand its Eindhoven team as it moves toward commercialisation.

content_en:
# Claude Science tackles deadly scorpion stings by designing protein binders from scratch

**Anthropic's Claude largely autonomously designed protein binders targeting scorpion neurotoxins, which kill more than 3,250 people every year.** These small protein molecules are shaped to latch onto a specific target molecule. Claude generated 318,484 designs for such protein binders targeting five toxins from four scorpion species. After an initial prompt, Claude worked on its own for 24 hours. The research team then steered the work with additional instructions.

Claude picked 180 candidates, and the team added 31 more. Of the 211 designs tested in the lab, 17 met the criteria for a binder. The two strongest bound extremely tightly to Cn2, a toxin from the Mexican scorpion. Lab tests suggest they dock at or near the same site as an antibody known to neutralize Cn2 in mice. Whether they actually work as an antivenom hasn't been tested yet.

External experts Susana Vázquez Torres and Timothy P. Jenkins called the work a promising first step. Two independent labs confirmed the results. Claude worked inside Claude Science, Anthropic's AI environment for researchers. In an earlier study, Claude had already designed mini-binders against 14 of 15 target proteins, with hit rates of 22 to 35 percent compared to the typical 10 to 15 percent.

Italian AI startup Rulen (formerly LexSA) has raised €1.8 million in its first funding round to further develop its AI-powered platform for the tax and accounting sector and support its commercial expansion. The round was led by VC Partners, with participation from Growth Engine, AME Ventures, Zest through its Magic Mind vehicle, Alpha Venture and a group of industry business angels.

Launched at the end of 2025, Rulen develops an AI operating platform designed to automate tax and accounting workflows, helping professionals reduce repetitive tasks and manage compliance processes more efficiently.

The platform integrates with existing software and third-party systems, including the Italian Revenue Agency's online taxpayer records (Cassetto Fiscale), allowing firms to automate processes from data collection to review and document production while maintaining professional oversight.

The company aims to address challenges facing the Italian tax and accounting sector, including a shortage of younger professionals and growing compliance workloads. New registrations in the profession have declined by 27.3 per cent, while professionals under 40 account for just 15 per cent of the sector. At the same time, many firms continue to rely on manual processes and fragmented software systems, increasing the need for automation tools that can support business growth without a proportional increase in staffing.

Rulen's platform is already used by law and tax firms, specialist practices, groups consolidating professional firms and multinational companies.

The funding announcement coincides with the company's rebranding from LexSA to Rulen, reflecting its transition from an AI research assistant to a platform capable of executing end-to-end workflows.

Simone Hong, co-founder and CEO of Rulen, explained that the company was created in response to challenges experienced directly by its founders, particularly the difficulty of recruiting junior professionals and the time spent on repetitive administrative work. He added:

Claudio Cama, co-founder and CTO of Rulen, highlighted the company's plans to expand automation across additional activities by integrating new systems and developing AI agents capable of handling execution tasks independently, allowing professionals to focus on higher-value decisions.

content_en:
**YGO**, a Berlin-based startup building an AI infrastructure layer for the travel industry, raised €8 million in a Series A round.

The round was led by Ventech, with participation from Sake Bosch, Caesar and Business Angels. In August 2024, the company announced it had secured €2.5 million in funding led by GetAway Group.

“*Online travel booking is undergoing its biggest structural shift in decades but most of the industry’s infrastructure was never built for it. YGO’s customers are already re-owning their customer relationships with AI and putting real KPI uplifts on the board to prove it. That’s why we believe YGO’s neutral infrastructure will become critical to how travel operates in an AI-first world*,” said **Nicolas Barthalon**, Partner at Ventech.

Founded in 2023 by Julian Kögel, Sebastian Kreutzberger, and Willi Ibbeken, YGO sits at the intersection of legacy travel technology and the emerging ecosystem of AI agents. The company’s platform connects travel companies, including tour operators, online travel agencies, and travel agencies, directly with airlines, hotels, and tour operator inventory, without the need to restructure their existing booking infrastructure.

YGO does this by structuring and enriching fragmented hotel and product data, giving it the depth and accuracy that AI agents need to reliably discover, compare and recommend travel products. Its content enrichment product automatically generates verified, structured hotel data and delivers it across a company’s own digital channels and to external AI assistants via MCP (Model Context Protocol).

Its Hotel Q&A product embeds an AI-powered question-and-answer layer directly onto hotel pages, allowing travellers to ask any question and receive verified answers in real time and in their own language. Its AI Distribution product, on the other hand, makes a travel company’s entire hotel portfolio accessible and bookable through AI agents such as ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini.

YGO says online travel agencies and metasearch platforms have captured 15-25% of every booking, acting as intermediaries between travellers and suppliers. With AI assistants becoming the starting point for travel planning and booking, suppliers are looking for ways to reclaim direct relationships with their customers.

The platform already processes bookings for major European travel players including Condor, Bentour, and GetAway Group. YGO says their collaboration has led to a 90% reduction in manual operations and a 20% improvement in conversion for one airline client, and a 2.4x increase in average order value with no additional headcount for another.

“*Travel is one of the last major industries still built on infrastructure that was never designed for an AI-first world. We built YGO to change that: to give the travel industry the infrastructure to make its inventory accessible, bookable and ready for AI – whether through their own platforms or through external AI agents*,” said **Kögel**, co-founder and CEO of YGO.

YGO has grown its recurring ARR into seven figures within six months and has processed more than €15 million in bookings through its infrastructure to date. The fresh capital will be utilised to scale go-to-market and sales operations, deepen its AI orchestration platform, and expand the company’s customer base beyond the DACH region, targeting both enterprise accounts and mid-sized travel companies.

“*This funding allows us to build on the strong business we already have with some of Europe’s leading travel players and become the AI infrastructure layer connecting the industry to the next generation of travel*,” added Kögel.

title: Investors are questioning neoclouds' business model but Nebius says AI computing prices are rising

title_en: Investors are questioning neoclouds' business model but Nebius says AI computing prices are rising
excerpt_en: The comments come as investors scrutinize the debt, borrowing costs and economics of companies building AI infrastructure.
content_en:
BERLIN — Nebius is seeing AI computing prices rise more than expected, a top executive told CNBC on Wednesday, offering a bullish view as neocloud firms' business model comes under increasing scrutiny**.**

Investors have grown wary after CoreWeave, one of the biggest neocloud players, saw its cost of borrowing spike. The CoreWeave developments and questions around the amount of debt being used to fund the data center buildout have weighed heavily on other neoclouds like Iren and Nebius, whose stocks have dropped sharply over the last month.

Marc Boroditsky, chief revenue officer at Nebius, said his company wasn't in CoreWeave's position because "we're not carrying the kind of debt that they are."

He also said that if the AI infrastructure company brought its 2027 capacity online, it would sell out. There could be "the same type of dynamic" in 2028, supporting a positive longer-term demand outlook, he said, as companies race to secure access to computing power.

When asked whether he sees the price per megawatt continuing to rise ahead of expectations, Boroditsky replied: "Yeah."

Nebius is among a new wave of Neocloud companies that are investing billions to buy up Nvidia's graphics processing units, build data centers and rent that capacity.

Nebius ran an auction for computing capacity on Tuesday, which showed continued price rises, the revenue chief said. "We're seeing continued upward mobility in terms of the kind of price per megawatt," he told CNBC.

Price per megawatt, a key measure among new cloud companies, shows how much a company can charge customers for a certain amount of computing capacity.

Chase Lochmiller, CEO of Crusoe, an Nvidia-backed AI company that is building data centers, was also bullish on pricing, saying the company was seeing rising prices for GPUs, including older Nvidia chips.

"We're seeing higher pricing today for A100s than we saw in 2020 or 2021. We're seeing higher pricing for H100s than what we saw when they were first deployed in 2023," Lochmiller said.

"There's tremendous demand and a lot of it is because the underlying model capabilities have gotten so much more advanced that people are just creating so much more value out of the compute infrastructure."

The comments come amid an investor debate over how quickly Nvidia's GPUs lose their economic value as more powerful chips enter the market.

The ability to continue renting out older chips at attractive prices is crucial to AI infrastructure companies that need to recover their investments and generate profits, while spending billions on GPUs.

Lochmiller's comments suggest that, at least for Crusoe, older generations of Nvidia chips are commanding higher rental prices than when they were first deployed, potentially strengthening the economics of its AI cloud business.

## SpaceX boost

Nebius stock rose on Wednesday after SpaceX reported revenue at its AI business jumped ninefold to $7.56 billion. SpaceX CFO Bret Johnsen said pricing is "currently tracking slightly above the high end of the $30 to $50 per watt range," underscoring the pricing power for those renting out compute capacity.

Cloud providers CoreWeave, Iren, and Applied Digital also rose in premarket trading on Wednesday following Johnsen's comments.

"I'm thrilled by SpaceX's results. It's confirming what we already know, which is that it's a very dynamic market and that supply continues to fall far behind demand," Boroditsky said.

title: Europe Wants Data Centers. Its Climate Goals Are Getting in the Way
excerpt: A plan to funnel the heat given off by data centers into nearby homes has run aground in Germany. Across Europe, policymakers are weighing AI ambitions against climate objectives.
title_en: Europe Wants Data Centers. Its Climate Goals Are Getting in the Way
excerpt_en: A plan to funnel the heat given off by data centers into nearby homes has run aground in Germany. Across Europe, policymakers are weighing AI ambitions against climate objectives.
content_en:
Earlier this year, the German government laid out an ambitious plan: By 2030, it would double the scale of the country’s data center fleet, and quadruple the amount of compute available for running artificial intelligence models. The idea was to minimize Germany’s dependence on the United States for access to AI—a point of concern across Europe—and boost its faltering economy.

However, Germany has found that its AI ambitions are butting up against its climate commitments. EU member states have committed to cutting greenhouse gas emissions by 55 percent by the end of the decade. But policies meant to help meet that target are interfering with attempts to trigger a data center building frenzy.

As part of its broader climate commitments, the previous German administration voted through the Energy Efficiency Act in 2023. Among other things, it required all new data centers to recycle a portion of the waste heat generated by their computer equipment, ideally into nearby municipal heating systems. It seemed like a no-brainer, says Patrick Graichen, who served as a senior official at Germany’s Ministry for Economic Affairs and Energy at the time, before resigning over cronyism allegations.

“We need clean heat, and data centers are a source of clean heat,” Graichen tells WIRED.

In June, a month before the rules were due to finally take effect, the German federal government walked them back. Data center firms had complained that the requirements made it almost impossible to build in the country; the German Data Center Association characterized an early version of the bill as a “data center prevention act.” Under an amended bill, which will be put to the German parliament for ratification imminently, data center operators would no longer be obligated to reuse waste heat, only to scope out the possibility.

Graichen and others have accused the German government of sacrificing climate targets for a chance to ride the AI wave. But countries across Europe find themselves pulled between these same two poles, under simultaneous pressure to cash in on rapid growth in the energy-intensive AI sector—and limit dependence on the US—and to protect the climate.

The German Ministry for Economic Affairs and Energy did not respond to a request for comment.

Among data center developers, the chief objection to the original Energy Efficiency Act was the chance it could land them in an impossible bind, obligated to reuse waste heat even when there was no available offtake—whether a municipal heating system or an industry, like greenhouse agriculture. “Some of the things they had to comply with were outside of their control,” says Barbara Smitten, associate director for critical systems at consulting firm Cundall. “It felt that \[the burden\] was all on the data center.”

In the last 18 months, multiple data center proposals have fallen through in Germany: Stack Infrastructure canceled a $3 billion facility in Hesse, and state-owned Komm.ONE withdrew from a project in Baden-Württemberg. Though precisely what causes a data center development to fold is rarely clear, Komm.ONE pointed directly to the burdens of the Energy Efficiency Act.

Graichen claims that the industry’s objections are groundless. He says the availability of a heat offtake should become a default criterion for any developer searching for a new site. “Stop complaining,” he says.

When an offtake is available, recycling heat produced by a data center is straightforward. “There is no technical reason why a data center cannot use its waste heat. The technologies and concepts are well known,” says John Booth, managing director at IT consultancy Carbon3IT, who helped to devise EU-wide energy efficiency targets for data centers. “There is absolutely no reason except the will of the organization to do it.”

Nevertheless, under the amended Energy Efficiency Act, data center developers are required only to assess whether recycling heat is economically and technically feasible. If not, they are exempt. “With practical rules for data centers, we are creating the conditions for digital sovereignty and economic growth,” wrote Katherina Reiche, federal minister for economic affairs and energy, when the cabinet approved the change.

The amendment may unlock pent-up demand among data center developers to build in Germany, whose geographic centrality makes it easy to route data efficiently into Western and Eastern Europe. “It lessens the risk of people not seeing the German market as attractive,” says Smitten.

But in a roundabout way, it could also undermine the aim to spark a building frenzy, inviting the type of climate-focused activism that has led to permitting freezes and data center moratoria in the US. Already, in February, the city council of a small German town voted to block the construction of a $2.5 billion data center development, partly over climate concerns.

As policymakers contend with conflicting ambitions to improve domestic AI capabilities and meet climate objectives, some say the swelling public unease about that trade-off will complicate things yet further in Europe. In the last year, the attitude toward data centers “has switched completely,” claims Graichen. “First and foremost in the US, but the same will happen in Europe.”
